title: Part II — ACCEPTANCE: Getting to Yes

know: What stands between a merchant and the issuer's answer: the acquirer of record and its license, the payment method and its scheme rules, the provider's model of the payment, the provider's actions inside the authorization call, the choice of provider, and, in a shop, the terminal.

What Stripe and Adyen have each documented, with dates, about acquiring entities, payment-method abstraction, payment state, optimization products, multi-provider routing and terminals, and what neither publishes.
believe: An approval is an outcome the provider and the merchant help produce, and its meaning depends on the payment method; it is not a verdict the network hands back.
An approval rate cannot be compared between providers until the acquirer, the method mix, the metric and its denominator are held equal.
can_do: Given a payment that was declined, delayed or approved and later taken back, say which layer decided it: acquirer and license, method, state model, optimization, routing or device.
Ask a provider, for one country, which entity acquires, which methods are final and when, what the synchronous answer does and does not promise, and how its published uplift was measured.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
Given an approval-rate complaint the part does not contain, a reader who has read only Part II names checks at three different layers before blaming the issuer.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A furniture retailer based in Sweden sells online in Sweden and Poland through one payment provider. Its dashboard shows that Polish debit cards are approved less often than Swedish ones. Using only Part II, name three things you would check before concluding that Polish banks are stricter.
acceptance_criteria.expected: At least three of: which legal entity acquires the Polish payments and whether the issuer sees them as domestic or cross-border; which rate is on the dashboard (authorization rate or checkout conversion, counted per attempt or per purchase); whether the provider's reformatting, retries or pre-network blocking apply to both countries alike; whether a local Polish payment method would carry some of these payments instead of a card. The answer does not treat the rate as a fact about Polish cardholders alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a 'succeeded' status on a payment method the reader has not met in the part, the reader asks what that status promises for that method before acting on it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A provider's API returns status 'succeeded' for a payment made by bank direct debit (the seller pulls the money from the buyer's bank account under a standing permission). A colleague wants to pay the seller out the same afternoon because 'the payment succeeded'. What does Part II tell you to say?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That 'succeeded' means a different promise per payment method: for a direct debit the buyer can take the money back for weeks without giving a reason, so the payout decision needs a rule per method family and cannot be read from the status word; and that the answer in the API response is not the final outcome.

thesis.question: What decides whether a payment gets to 'yes', and what can a provider or a merchant do about it?
thesis.claim: A 'yes' is produced in layers that sit around the issuer's decision: the licensed entity that acquires the payment, the payment method and what its scheme lets 'yes' mean, the provider's model of the payment between request and outcome, the changes and retries the provider makes inside the authorization call, the choice among providers, and, when the card is in the room, the terminal. Each layer changes how often the answer is yes or whether that yes can later be taken back. The provider holds the license and makes the changes inside the call; the merchant chooses the methods it offers, the providers it uses and the devices it deploys; so an approval is an outcome both help produce.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that approval is the issuer's verdict on the cardholder and the provider is a neutral pipe to the network, so that the approval rate would be the same on any provider and a 'yes' means the same thing for every payment method.
thesis.so_what: A team that accepts the claim stops reading its approval rate as a fact about its customers. It asks which layer produced a decline before changing anything, and it does not compare two providers' rates or published uplift figures without first lining up the acquirer, the method mix and the metric.
thesis.how_why: The issuer decides on what reaches it: a payment that arrives as domestic or cross-border, on one network or another, with a card number or a network token, formatted one way or another, once or after a retry. Every one of those inputs is set before the issuer sees the message, by the license the provider holds or borrows, by the method chosen at checkout, and by code the provider runs inside the call. For methods that are not cards there may be no issuer answer at all, only a scheme rule about when the money is final. Stripe and Adyen document different arrangements at most of these layers, and neither publishes a list of its network memberships by network and country, volume per acquirer or an audited approval lift; the part's argument rests on what they do publish.

supporting_claims.claim: Reaching a card network takes a membership held by a licensed entity, so the acquirer of record is a legal fact that differs by country and decides how a payment arrives at the issuer and how many parties stand between the merchant and the network.
What 'yes' promises is fixed by each payment method's scheme, so one API can unify how a payment is started and reported and cannot unify what its success means.
The outcome of a payment is a state reached over time, so a payment must be modeled as a record with explicit states in which the synchronous response is one transition and not the result.

Providers now reformat, retry, reroute and block inside the authorization call, so the approval rate is partly the provider's product, and the uplift figures published for it cannot be compared or verified from public data.
Routing across providers unifies the authorization request and nothing after it, so a second provider is paid for in per-provider disputes, settlement, records and stored cards.

When the card is present, approval and fraud liability depend on a managed device and the chip data it passes on, and treating store and online payments as one has to be built from shared identifiers, refunds and reports.

role.contribution: Shows that the first promise of Part I, the authorization, is shaped before it reaches the issuer by how the provider is connected and how it models the payment, and supplies the payment state model that the ledger (Part III) and the API (Part IV) build on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: acquiring-and-network-connectivity to payment-state-machines: from the legal entity and its networks, to the payment method, to the single payment record
authorization-optimization to payment-routing-and-orchestration: declines and what one provider does about them, then the proposal to add a second provider

flow.rationale: The chapters follow the order in which a 'yes' is constrained. Connectivity comes first because the acquirer decides which networks and local schemes can be reached at all; methods come second because they are what those connections carry and they show that 'yes' has more than one meaning; the state machine comes third because it is the model that holds both the card's instant answer and the other methods' late ones. Only with attempts and states defined can chapter 9 explain several network attempts behind one API call and say what an approval rate counts, and only with one provider's levers known can chapter 10 weigh a second provider against them. In-person payments come last because the chapter reuses every earlier term (acquirer, method, state, offline authorization as a deferred attempt) with a device added. Moving optimization ahead of the state machine would ask the reader to follow a retry before knowing what a payment attempt is; moving routing ahead of optimization would compare providers on a rate the reader cannot yet define. Three of the six transitions are contrasts or problem-solution moves; the chapter 9 step is an elaboration because it unpacks the 'attempt' the state machine named.

hook.content: At 1,140 Larkfield studios in the Netherlands and Germany, a member who renews her membership online is charged through Stripe, and the same member tapping the same card at the front desk is charged through Adyen. One card, one studio, one bank deciding; two providers, two routes to that bank, and two records of what 'approved' meant.

opening.bridge: From Part I's view of the authorization as a message that goes to the issuer and comes back with an answer, to the provider's side of that message: who is allowed to send it, in what form, how many times, and what the answer is recorded as.
opening.roadmap: Six chapters in the order a 'yes' is constrained: who acquires the payment and under which license; what 'yes' means for methods that are not cards; how a payment is modeled as states; why issuers decline and what providers do inside the call; when a second provider helps and what it costs; and what changes when the card is in the room.

closing.synthesis: Each layer of a 'yes' has a different owner: the license holder decides how the payment arrives at the issuer, the scheme decides what the answer promises, the provider's model decides how the wait is shown, the provider's optimizer decides how many attempts sit behind one call, the merchant decides how many providers, and at the counter the device decides what data the issuer gets. No single chapter says what follows from putting them side by side: an approval rate describes the whole stack, so it belongs to a provider, a country and a method together and cannot be moved from one setup to another.
closing.so_what: Larkfield's Keel decision K8 follows from this: it keeps two providers and one rehearsed switch and adds no orchestration product, because at its volume the gain is in knowing each stack, and a routing layer would unify the request while leaving two sets of disputes, settlements and stored cards.
closing.callback: The 1,140 studios whose members are charged through Stripe online and through Adyen at the front desk: the same card meets two stacks, and the terminal on the counter is the last layer of one of them.

takeaway.content: For each provider and country, write down the acquiring entity, each payment method with the date its payments become final, the provider states your own record mirrors, the approval metric with its denominator, and the date the switch to the other provider was last rehearsed.

transition_in.carries_over: Part I's parties and timeline, the authorization as the issuer's promise and the first of several, and the fee stack that makes an approved payment worth more to every party than a declined one.
transition_in.introduces: The path to that first promise, which Part I took as given: the acquirer and its license, the payment method, the provider's model of the payment and the provider's own actions before the issuer answers.

posts.title: Part II — ACCEPTANCE: Getting to Yes
posts.question: What does Part II argue about how a payment gets approved, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part II answers six questions in order: who acquires the payment, what 'yes' means per payment method, how a payment is modeled as states, why issuers decline and what providers do about it, when to use more than one provider, and what changes at a terminal.
believe: An approval is produced in layers around the issuer's decision, and each layer has a different owner.
can_do: Pick the Part II chapter that addresses a decline, a late outcome or a provider question in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can state the part's claim and name the six chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does Part II claim about approvals, and what will each of the next six chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a 'yes' is shaped by layers around the issuer's decision and is not a verdict handed back by the network; then acquiring and licenses, payment methods other than cards, the payment state machine, declines and optimization, routing across providers, in-person payments.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens with the 1,140 Larkfield studios charged through Stripe online and through Adyen at the front desk, with the figures as the scenario ledger gives them.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis, links it to the authorization of Part I and gives the reading order.

posts.title: Plugging Into the Networks: Acquiring, Licences and Connectivity
posts.question: What does it take to connect to the card networks and local schemes, and what separates Adyen's route to them (one banking license) from Stripe's (licenses and partner banks assembled market by market)?

know: What an acquirer, a sponsor bank, a processor, a gateway and a payment facilitator each are, and which of them holds the network membership.

The licenses Adyen states it holds and their years (EU banking license 2017, US federal branch 2021, UK authorization 2023), and the acquirer Stripe names per country in its acquirer disclosure (its own entities in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific, named partner banks and its own limited-purpose bank in the United States).
What neither company publishes: a list of network memberships by network and country, volume per acquirer, and a current list of direct connections.
believe: A direct technical connection to a network and being the acquirer of record are different facts, and a provider can have the first without the second.
That domestic payments are approved more often and cost less than cross-border ones is accepted in the industry, and the size of the effect is not publicly measured.
can_do: For a given provider and country, find out which entity is the acquirer of record and say what follows for the flow of funds and for who answers to the network.
Read a provider's 'direct connection' or 'local acquiring' claim and say what it does and does not establish.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a provider statement about connectivity, the reader separates the technical connection from the acquirer of record and names what to ask next.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A payment company's website says it has 'direct integrations with Visa and Mastercard' in Canada. Its legal pages say it is a 'payment facilitator' (a company that signs up many merchants under another institution's network membership) of a named Canadian bank. Using only this chapter: who is the acquirer for a Canadian merchant, and what does the 'direct integration' sentence tell you?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The named bank is the acquirer of record: it holds the membership and answers to the network, and settlement funds pass through it. The direct integration means the company exchanges messages with the networks itself; it says nothing about who holds the membership or the liability.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a claimed approval gain from local acquiring, the reader says the direction is accepted, the size is vendor-reported, and what a sound measurement would need.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A sales deck promises 'a 3% authorization uplift from local acquiring', citing one customer. Using only this chapter, how much weight do you give the number, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Little: domestic payments being approved more often than cross-border ones is accepted, but no independent measurement of the size is public; the cited figures are single-customer cases that bundle local acquiring with other changes and give no baseline.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about Stripe's or Adyen's licenses, acquirers and connections carries its year or access date, and the chapter says in plain words where the public record stops.

thesis.question: What does it take to connect to the card networks and local schemes, and what separates Adyen's route to them (one banking license) from Stripe's (licenses and partner banks assembled market by market)?
thesis.claim: Connecting to a card network takes a membership that only a licensed entity can hold, so every payment has an acquirer of record that differs by country and that decides whether the issuer sees a domestic payment and where the money flows. Adyen obtained one banking license in 2017 and extended it through branches, while Stripe is its own acquirer under e-money licenses in the EEA and the UK and a payment facilitator under named acquirers, most of them banks, in markets such as the United States: both are ways of holding that membership, and what separates them is how many parties stand between the merchant and the network: none where the provider is itself the acquirer, a sponsoring acquirer where it is not.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that connectivity is a technical integration: a provider that sends messages straight to Visa and Mastercard is connected, and the licenses behind it are legal paperwork with no effect on approvals, cost or where the money flows.
thesis.so_what: A team evaluating a provider asks, per country, which entity acquires its payments, because that entity decides whether the issuer sees a domestic payment, adds or removes a settlement hop, and is the party whose rules and failures the merchant inherits. 'Which provider' is the wrong unit; 'which acquirer in this country' is the right one.
thesis.how_why: Visa defines an acquirer as a member that signs the merchant and enters transactions 'directly or indirectly', so membership and the technical link are separate. Stripe shows both sides: in April 2020 it announced direct integrations with six card networks, and its acquirer disclosure (read November 2026) still names five partner banks and its own limited-purpose Georgia bank as US acquirers, with Stripe entities as acquirer in the EEA and the UK. Adyen states that its licenses give it direct network access and that 84% of its 2025 volume was 'full-stack', and its annual report places concentration risk at banking partners 'in locations where there are no own direct acquiring licenses', which the chapter reads, as an inference, as reliance on partners there. Adyen's stated reason for its route is 'the speed and autonomy that come from not relying on external parties' (annual report for 2025); Stripe has published no comparable account of why it chose its route, so the chapter compares what the two routes are and does not claim to know Stripe's reasons. The comparison is the author's inference. Neither publishes a list of its network memberships by network and country, volume per acquirer or a current list of direct connections, and no independent figure exists for the approval gain from local acquiring, so the chapter argues from the entities and stops there.

role.contribution: Establishes who is allowed to send a payment to a network and under whose name, which is the first constraint on every later chapter's 'yes'.

transition_in.carries_over: The part intro's claim that a 'yes' is shaped in layers before the issuer decides, and Part I's acquirer as one box in the four-party model.
transition_in.introduces: What is inside that box: a network membership, the license that permits it, and the different ways Stripe and Adyen hold both.

posts.title: A Payment Is Not a Card: Local Methods and Real-Time Rails
posts.question: How does one API accept a hundred payment methods whose semantics differ?

know: The payment method families and the properties on which they differ from cards: who starts the payment, when the outcome is known, whether there is a hold to capture, whether and for how long the payer can take the money back, how a refund travels, whether a mandate is needed, and when funds settle.

How Stripe (a PaymentMethod object with a type; dynamic payment methods by default since API version 2023-08-16) and Adyen (a method type passed to the Checkout API, a documented flow type and capture mode per method, methods configured on the merchant account) each present methods through one API.
believe: A status of 'succeeded' is a different promise for a card, a bank redirect and a direct debit, and no provider can change that because the scheme sets it.
'Real-time' describes how fast the payer's money moves, not whether the payment is final for the merchant or when the merchant has the funds.
can_do: Given a payment method they have not used, list the questions that decide what their system may do after 'succeeded' and find the answers in a provider's method page.
Write a per-method-family policy (grant access, pay out, expect a reversal until when) instead of branching on the status alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a method the chapter does not walk through, the reader asks the questions that separate it from a card before deciding how to fulfill and pay out.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your company will start accepting a voucher method: the customer gets a barcode at checkout and pays cash at a convenience store within three days. Using only this chapter, list four questions you must answer before deciding when to ship the order and how refunds will work.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Four of: when and how the outcome is confirmed (days later or never, by webhook, not in the API response); whether there is any authorization or hold to capture (no, one step); whether the payer can take the money back afterwards and until when; how a refund is sent when there is no card to reverse to and whether it can fail; when funds settle; what the customer must do next and what happens if they do not.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two providers' terms for the same scheme event, the reader recognizes them as one rule and maps them to a neutral term of their own.
acceptance_criteria.probe: For a returned direct debit, one provider's report shows a 'dispute' and another's shows a 'chargeback'; the second provider also shows a 'chargeback' when the customer's account simply had no money. A dashboard adds these up as 'fraud disputes'. What is wrong, using only this chapter?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The two words name the same scheme event in different vocabularies, and an unpaid debit is a failed collection, not a customer dispute; summing them overstates disputes. The integration needs its own terms that separate a payer's refund claim, an unauthorized-debit claim and a failed collection.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Scheme rules are attributed to the scheme or the law with their dates, provider behavior to the provider's documentation with its date, and items in preview or migration (iDEAL to Wero) are marked as likely to change.

thesis.question: How does one API accept a hundred payment methods whose semantics differ?
thesis.claim: One API accepts many payment methods by unifying how a payment is started and how its status is reported; it cannot unify what 'succeeded' means, because when the outcome is known, whether there is a hold to capture and whether the payer can take the money back are fixed by each scheme. The integration therefore has to carry a rule per method family for what it may do after 'succeeded'.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the provider's abstraction is complete: once every method sits behind the same call and the same status field, the integration can treat them alike, and the differences are edge cases the provider absorbs.
thesis.so_what: A team that grants access, ships or pays a seller out on the status word alone has built the failure pattern A Card by Any Other Name. On a platform the cost lands in balances: a payment that can be taken back for weeks needs a payout rule that knows which method carried it.
thesis.how_why: The scheme rules differ in kind. An iDEAL payment cannot be disputed through the payer's bank; a SEPA direct debit can be refunded without a reason for eight weeks and contested as unauthorized for thirteen months under PSD2 (2015, still in force), and is confirmed days after submission. Stripe's documentation says in general terms that a succeeded payment 'can still be refunded, disputed, returned, or reversed'. The two providers present the variety differently: Stripe stores the instrument as a PaymentMethod object and, by default since API version 2023-08-16, chooses which methods to show per session; Adyen takes the method as a parameter, returns the methods configured on the merchant account, and documents a flow type and a capture mode (immediate or separate) per method. They also name the same scheme event differently, a 'dispute' at Stripe and a 'chargeback' at Adyen. Neither publishes a list of the methods it reaches through another payment company (single method pages name a partner), so the chapter describes the contract each documents and not what is behind it.

role.contribution: Shows that 'yes' has more than one meaning, so that the state model of the next chapter and every later use of 'approved' carries the method with it.

transition_in.carries_over: The acquirer and its network memberships, described for cards, and the observation that some local schemes can be reached only by a local acquirer or entity.
transition_in.introduces: Payments that are not cards: methods with no issuer answer, no hold or no chargeback, where what the provider connects to changes what 'approved' promises.

posts.title: One Object, Many Outcomes: The Payment State Machine
posts.question: How do you model a payment that can be pending, need a customer action, succeed later, be partly captured and partly refunded?

know: Why a single charge request with a yes-or-no answer could not represent payments that need a customer action or are confirmed later, as Stripe described it in 2020.

The states of Stripe's PaymentIntent (introduced 2018) and how a failed attempt returns it to an earlier state; Adyen's result codes, action objects (since Checkout API v49, May 2019) and modifications as separate asynchronous requests.
What a payment state machine must guarantee: one terminal outcome, only legal transitions, and transitions that are safe to apply twice.
believe: Waiting for the customer and waiting for the network are different states, and the synchronous API response is one transition, not the outcome.
A consumer should keep the provider's status as received and derive its own smaller vocabulary from it.
can_do: Design a payment record that mirrors two providers with different models: one that offers an object to re-read and one that reports results per request and by webhook.
Given an event that arrives late, twice or out of order, say which transition is legal and which must be ignored.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a payment flow the chapter does not contain, the reader places each moment in a state and says which system's message moves it on.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer pays by scanning a QR code with their banking app. The API call returns at once with the code to display; the customer scans it four minutes later; the bank confirms a few seconds after that; the customer has already closed the browser tab. Using only this chapter: which states does your payment record pass through, and what triggers the last transition?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A state for waiting on the customer's action after the first response, then a state for waiting on the bank or network, then a terminal success; the last transition is triggered by the provider's server-side notification (or by fetching the provider's record), never by the browser returning, because the customer may not come back.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a late contradictory event, the reader applies the guarantees: one terminal outcome, legal transitions only, repeated events harmless.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your record shows a payment as captured. Two days later the provider sends an event saying the capture failed. A minute later the same event arrives again. What should your state machine do with each, according to this chapter?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Accept the first as a legal transition out of a state that was never final (a successful capture response is itself a promise), move the payment to the failed-capture state and trigger whatever depends on it; treat the second as a repeat that changes nothing. The reader does not discard the event as impossible.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's account of Stripe's redesign is dated to its 2020 source with its age stated, Adyen's model is described from its documentation and API specification, and the absence of a comparable Adyen design history is said outright.

thesis.question: How do you model a payment that can be pending, need a customer action, succeed later, be partly captured and partly refunded?
thesis.claim: Such a payment has to be modeled as one long-lived record that moves through explicit states, with waiting for the customer and waiting for the network as separate states and the synchronous response as one transition among several; captures and refunds are separate operations recorded against that record, each for its own amount and with its own outcome. Stripe and Adyen both arrived at this model and expose it differently: Stripe as a PaymentIntent that can be retrieved and retried (2018), Adyen as a result code per request, follow-up operations as separate asynchronous requests and outcomes by webhook, with no endpoint in its Checkout API that returns a payment by its identifier.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a payment is a request with a yes-or-no answer, and that pending, action-required and partial outcomes are exceptions to cover with a few extra status values on the charge record.
thesis.so_what: The integrator's own payment record is designed, not copied: it stores each provider's status as received, maps it to a small vocabulary of its own (Larkfield's five states), accepts a state change only from the provider's confirmed record, and tolerates late and repeated events. With two providers, one side is read from an object and the other is assembled from results and events.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's own account (December 2020, six years old) is that its Charge was built for US cards, which finalize at once with no customer action; a pending state was added in 2015 for bank debits, a client-driven object followed, and payments went uncompleted and were refunded when the browser lost its connection, so in 2018 it introduced an intent with states for customer action and for processing and with no failed state, since a failed attempt returns the intent to where a new attempt can be made. Adyen's documentation shows the same shape reached by another route: an action object in responses since May 2019, a recommendation not to update order systems from the result code, and captures and refunds that are answered 'received' and can still fail days after a webhook reported success. Adyen has published no design history comparable to Stripe's: a knowledge-hub post of 5 October 2021 gives the reason for `/sessions` (API calls 'reduced from three to only one'), an engineering post of July 2021 gives the reason for asynchronous modifications (it keeps the edge layer stateless), and its reasons for result codes are not on record; the difference in what the integrator must store is the author's inference from the two documented contracts.

role.contribution: Supplies the model (attempt, state, transition, terminal outcome) that the optimization and routing chapters count in and that Parts III and IV record and expose.

transition_in.carries_over: The payment methods of the previous chapter, which differ in whether the customer must act and whether the outcome arrives now or days later.
transition_in.introduces: The one model that holds all of them: a payment as a record with states, and the two ways Stripe and Adyen present that record to an integrator.

posts.title: Raising the Approval Rate: Retries, Tokens and Optimization
posts.question: Why are payments from genuine cardholders with funds available declined, and what do providers do about it?

know: Who can stop a payment (the issuer, the provider before the network, an invalid request) and why most issuer declines carry no usable reason.
The difference between authorization rate, payment success rate and checkout conversion, and between counting per attempt and per purchase.

The levers that move approvals (local acquiring, network tokens, account updater, authentication choices, message formatting, retries within network limits, timing) and what Stripe's Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance and Adyen's Uplift are documented to do, with their dates and published claims.
believe: One API call can now stand for several network attempts, or for none, because the provider decides inside the call.
A published uplift figure is a vendor estimate on an unstated cohort and baseline until the merchant measures it on its own traffic with a randomized holdout.
can_do: State an approval metric with its numerator, denominator, cohort and counting rule before comparing two periods or two providers.
Design a test of an optimization feature with a holdout and guardrails for fraud, fees and blocked payments.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a reported improvement, the reader identifies what is missing before the number can be trusted.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your provider's account manager reports: 'After we enabled our optimization suite in March, your approval rate rose from 91.2% to 93.0%.' Using only this chapter, name four things you need to know before accepting that the suite caused a 1.8-point gain.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Four of: which rate (authorization rate or payment success rate) and what is excluded from the denominator; whether attempts or purchases are counted (retries inflate or deflate the raw rate); which cohort (first payments or renewals, which countries, card-not-present only); what else changed between the periods (season, card mix, issuer behavior), since this is a before-and-after comparison and not a randomized holdout; whether blocked-before-network payments moved out of the denominator; what happened to fraud, disputes and fees.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an outcome that never reached the issuer, the reader classifies it correctly and says how it affects the metrics.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A payment comes back as 'blocked: low probability of authorization, not sent to network'. Is this an issuer decline? What does it do to your authorization rate and to your count of lost sales, according to this chapter?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It is not an issuer decline: the provider stopped it before the network, usually to avoid a fee. It leaves the authorization-rate denominator, so that rate can rise while sales do not; it still counts as a failed purchase in the payment success rate, and some blocked payments would have been approved.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every uplift figure from Stripe or Adyen is quoted with its wording, source and date and is labeled a vendor claim; the chapter states that the two companies' figures use different metrics and cannot be compared.

thesis.question: Why are payments from genuine cardholders with funds available declined, and what do providers do about it?
thesis.claim: Payments from genuine cardholders with funds available are declined because each issuer decides alone, by its own reading of the authorization message, and usually returns no reason the merchant can act on; providers respond by acting inside the authorization call, where they reformat the message, swap the card number for a network token, retry, switch network or block the payment before it is sent. The approval rate is therefore partly the provider's product, and the uplift Stripe and Adyen each publish for it (Stripe: an acceptance rate 3.8% higher on average, stated in 2025; Adyen: payment conversion up to 6% higher in a pilot reported in January 2025) rests on different metrics, cohorts and baselines, so the two figures can be neither compared nor checked from public data.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a decline is the issuer's verdict on the cardholder, so the provider is a neutral pipe, the approval rate would be the same anywhere, and optimization products are packaging around a number nobody controls; or the opposite view, that a vendor's published uplift is what a merchant should expect to gain.
thesis.so_what: The merchant's system has to tolerate one call that produced several network attempts, a 'blocked' result that never reached a bank, and a credential or network other than the one it asked for. And the merchant, not the vendor, has to measure: fix the metric and denominator, hold out randomized traffic, wait for retries to finish, and watch fraud, fees and blocked payments in the same test.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's guide describes issuers combining the fields of the authorization message each in their own way and classing most refusals as generic. Against that, both providers document actions the merchant did not request: Stripe's Adaptive Acceptance reformats and retries within the original request and, for accounts on interchange-plus pricing, blocks payments unlikely to succeed; Adyen's Uplift (January 2025) routes, adjusts messaging, retries and can block excessive retries. Both describe machine-learned models (Stripe a deep network replacing gradient-boosted trees, February 2025; Adyen several models coordinated by reinforcement learning with a 20-millisecond median budget each, January 2025) beside settings the merchant controls. On measurement, Stripe documents a modeled per-payment estimate and previewed a 30-day randomized test in April 2026; Adyen describes a control group that still receives a 'market baseline'. Neither publishes features, labels, per-issuer results, the cost of wrongly blocked payments or an audited lift, Visa's reattempt limit is confirmed from its rules of 24 October 2026 (20 in 30 days) while Mastercard's is known only from secondary sources, so the chapter argues from the documented behavior and says where the numbers are vendor claims.

role.contribution: Shows the provider as an actor inside the authorization, which makes the approval rate a property of the provider's stack and gives the routing chapter the metric it compares providers on.

transition_in.carries_over: The state machine's distinction between a payment and its attempts: a failed attempt returns the payment to a state from which another attempt can be made.
transition_in.introduces: Why attempts fail at the issuer, who makes the next attempt and with what changes, and how an approval rate should be counted once one payment can hold several attempts.

posts.title: More Than One Provider: Routing and Orchestration
posts.question: When and how should payments be routed across acquirers or providers, and what does it cost?

know: The difference between routing inside one provider (among acquirers and networks, including least-cost routing of US debit) and routing across providers, and the ways to do the second: an in-house payment service, a dedicated orchestrator, or one provider's orchestration product.

What Stripe documents for routing to other processors (Orchestration, announced May 2025 and in private preview in November 2026; Vault and Forward) with its stated exclusions, and what Adyen documents (routing among acquirers and networks, a forward endpoint for stored cards, a multi pay-in pilot for platforms) and that no Adyen product for routing payments to other providers was found.
Why stored cards and network tokens are the hard part of leaving or adding a provider.
believe: A routing layer unifies the authorization request; disputes, settlement, balances, method coverage and stored cards remain one set per provider.
First-attempt routing needs evidence per segment that a small or mid-sized business does not have, and below that scale a simple rule with a rehearsed switch is the sound design.
can_do: For a stated business, decide between one provider, two providers with a rehearsed switch, and rule-based routing, and list what each adds to operations.
Write the exit questions to settle before adding a second provider: who holds the card vault, under whose identifier network tokens are issued, and how cards leave.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a business the chapter does not contain, the reader chooses a multi-provider stage and justifies it by volume per segment and operating cost, not by the number of providers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A language-learning app takes 400,000 card payments a year, 85% of them in two countries, through one provider that had two short outages last year. The CTO proposes buying an orchestration product and routing each payment to whichever of three providers has the best approval rate. Using only this chapter, what do you recommend and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Not rule-based routing across three: the volume per issuer or segment is too small to choose routes on evidence, and each provider adds its own integration, disputes, settlement, reconciliation and warm-up. The outages argue for a second provider with a plain, rehearsed failover and a settled answer on where the cards are stored; an orchestrator also becomes a new single point of failure and an extra hop.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a cross-provider retry, the reader says when it is safe.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A payment to provider A times out with no answer. Your routing layer is configured to retry failed payments on provider B. Should it retry this one? Answer from this chapter.
acceptance_criteria.expected: No, not yet: a timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure. A retry on another provider is safe only when the first attempt is known to have failed; otherwise the customer can be charged twice across two providers that cannot see each other. Find out the first attempt's outcome first.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Products in preview or pilot are labeled as such with the date checked, the merchant evidence is attributed to the one public account it comes from, and the chapter says that no audited comparison of multi-provider and single-provider approval rates is public.

thesis.question: When and how should payments be routed across acquirers or providers, and what does it cost?
thesis.claim: Routing each payment across providers pays for itself only where a business has enough payments in each segment (issuer, country, card type) for a difference in approval rate between routes to be measurable; below that, the use of a second provider is a failover that is triggered deliberately and has been rehearsed. In both cases the routing layer unifies the authorization request and nothing after it: disputes, settlement, balances, method coverage and stored cards stay one set per provider, and running those sets is what a second provider costs.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that several providers mean higher approval and lower risk, so a business that can afford it should put an orchestration layer in front of several providers and send each payment to the best performer.
thesis.so_what: Before adding a provider, a team decides who holds the card vault and how cards and network tokens leave it, staffs a second back office for disputes and settlement, and keeps the routing rule as simple as its evidence allows. Larkfield's rule, 'the studio's provider' with a rehearsed switch (K8), is the claim applied.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's documentation for its own Orchestration product lists what routing does not carry: disputes and settlement stay in the other processor's dashboard, non-card methods and several Stripe products are excluded, a routed payment creates no balance movement at Stripe, and a failed payment is not retried on another processor once 3-D Secure has been attempted. The one detailed merchant account found, given by Canva at a Stripe event in 2026, reports that the gain came from where traffic is sent first and that the price was about six months per provider integration, months of warming up each merchant account and close to thirty people. On the two companies: Stripe offers routing to other processors, Adyen among them, in private preview since May 2025, and a forwarding proxy out of its vault; Adyen documents routing among acquirers and networks (a US debit product since September 2024), a forward endpoint and a multi pay-in pilot, and no product for routing payments to other providers was found. That Stripe is willing to be the control layer over competitors and Adyen is not is the author's reading of those documents. Adyen's terms (13 June 2025) describe a service that shares network tokens for use with other payment providers, with the cryptogram still supplied by Adyen; no Stripe statement on whether its tokens can follow a merchant was found, and the scale at which routing pays is not publicly quantified.

role.contribution: Tests the obvious remedy for dependence on one provider's stack and shows what remains per provider when the request is unified, which is the money and the records that Part III takes up.

transition_in.carries_over: Every lever of the previous chapter sits inside one provider, whose decisions the merchant cannot inspect and whose outage stops every payment.
transition_in.introduces: The proposed remedy, a second provider and a layer that routes between them, with what it unifies, what it leaves per provider and when a simple switch is enough.

posts.title: The Card in the Room: Terminals and Unified Commerce
posts.question: What changes when the card is physically present, and what does it take to treat a store payment and an online payment as one?

know: What the chip adds (a one-time cryptogram per transaction), what the networks' liability rules make depend on it, and the two meanings of 'offline': approval by the card on the issuer's preset terms, and store-and-forward at the merchant's risk.

The integration shapes for terminals (local or cloud at Adyen on the nexo retail protocol; SDK or server-driven at Stripe with the same PaymentIntent as online) and what each does when the connection drops.

What 'unified commerce' consists of in data terms, and what each company publishes about its in-person business (Adyen reports point-of-sale volume, 22% of processed volume in 2025; Stripe publishes none).
believe: A terminal is a managed computer in the payment path, with software, keys and certificates that someone must own.

Using one provider for both channels does not by itself make a store payment and an online payment one; a shared shopper identifier, a cross-channel refund and a single settlement report each have to be checked.
can_do: Choose a terminal integration shape for a stated store network and say what it does offline and who carries that risk.
Test a provider's unified-commerce claim with three separate checks: recognizing the same payer across channels, refunding across channels, and reconciling both channels in one report.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an offline requirement the chapter does not contain, the reader distinguishes the two mechanisms and states who bears the loss on a later decline.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A ferry operator sells food on board with no connectivity for forty minutes per crossing. It wants to keep taking cards. Using only this chapter: what are its two options for an offline payment, and who loses the money if a stored payment is declined when the ferry docks?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Either the card itself approves on terms its issuer preset (not supported by most debit cards), or the terminal stores the payment and asks for authorization later (store-and-forward). In the second case the operator has already handed over the goods and bears the loss on a decline, so limits per transaction and per device are the operator's credit decision; stored payments need their own retry and reconciliation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a 'unified commerce' claim, the reader breaks it into the three checks and does not accept one as proof of the others.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A provider says: 'With us, online and in-store payments are unified.' A shoe retailer wants to let customers return online orders in its shops for a refund to the original card. Using only this chapter, which three things do you verify, and which one does this use case depend on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A shared identifier for the same payer or card across channels; a refund path that works from one channel to a payment made in the other; one settlement report covering both. The return case depends on the cross-channel refund, and passing the other two does not prove it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's closing section performs the part's closing: it puts the six layers of a 'yes' side by side, states what follows for comparing approval rates, and returns to the 1,140 Larkfield studios charged through Stripe online and Adyen at the front desk.

Liability rules are attributed to the network rules actually read (Visa, with their edition date) and Mastercard's are marked as not verified; terminal models, country lists and volumes carry their dates; the chapter says that neither company publishes its terminal key management, and that Adyen documents how it rolls out terminal software releases (every four weeks, gradually) while Stripe documents no equivalent.

thesis.question: What changes when the card is physically present, and what does it take to treat a store payment and an online payment as one?
thesis.claim: When the card is present, a device joins the payment path: whether a fraud loss falls on the issuer or the merchant's side depends on the terminal reading the chip and the acquirer passing the chip data on, and a payment taken offline is credit the merchant extends. Treating a store payment and an online payment as one takes three things that have to be built and checked separately, a shared identifier for the payer, a refund path across channels and one settlement report; Stripe approaches them by reusing its online payment object at the counter, Adyen by shared references on one platform reached through a retail-industry terminal protocol.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a terminal is a card reader, an input device for the same payment, and that 'unified commerce' follows automatically from buying online and in-store payments from one provider.
thesis.so_what: A platform that puts terminals in its customers' shops takes on a device estate: inventory, software versions, keys and certificates per site, offline limits with a named owner, and a reconciliation path for stored payments. And it tests each of the three unified-commerce properties on its own, because a provider can deliver one without the others.
thesis.how_why: The chip produces a one-time cryptogram, and Visa's published rules (edition of October 2026) let an issuer push a counterfeit-fraud loss to the acquirer when the transaction did not take place at a chip-reading device or the full chip data was not transmitted; Mastercard's rules were not read and are described only as industry knowledge. Offline has two documented forms: Adyen supports approval by the card and store-and-forward with limits the merchant sets, Stripe store-and-forward only with a ceiling it enforces. In store-and-forward, authorization is attempted only after the connection returns, so the goods have left before any issuer has answered, which is why the chapter calls it credit extended by the merchant. The integration shapes differ in the same direction: Adyen's Terminal API follows the nexo retail protocol and runs locally or through the cloud; Stripe drives readers from an SDK or its own API and represents the payment as the PaymentIntent used online, with a generated card for reuse, since Stripe documents that a card read in person cannot itself be reused online. That the shared identifier, the cross-channel refund and the single report are separable, so that a provider can deliver one without the others, is the author's judgement and not a documented finding about either company. Adyen has designed terminals in-house since 2022 and reports point-of-sale volume (22% of processed volume in 2025); Stripe publishes no in-person volume. That Adyen exposes more of the card-present toolkit and Stripe one safer default is the author's reading; neither publishes key management or failure rates, and only Adyen documents how terminal software updates are rolled out.

role.contribution: Adds the device to the layers of a 'yes' and carries the part's closing, where the six layers are set side by side and the part hands off to the question of where the approved money is recorded.

transition_in.carries_over: Every chapter so far assumed a payment made at a distance, where the provider's software is the only thing between the merchant and the network, and the previous chapter's finding that a platform may run one provider online and another at the counter.
transition_in.introduces: The card in the room: a physical device in the payment path, liability that turns on what it reads and transmits, and the work of joining a counter payment to an online one.
